analysis.one_liner: Directs the FDA to study and ease rules for substituting cheaper copies of expensive biologic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs (complex medicines made from living cells) can cost thousands of dollars per dose, and cheaper copies called 'interchangeable biologics' can be swapped in at the pharmacy without a new prescription, the way generic pills are. This bill would have required the FDA to study whether confusing differences between the biologic and generic drug rating systems slow down those swaps, report to Congress, and update the FDA's official list of approved biologics (the 'Purple Book') to make substitutability clearer. It was a study-and-update bill, not a mandate: it would not have directly forced any price cut, but it aimed at removing paperwork and communication barriers that keep cheaper copies from being used. The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs, and the employers and insurers who help pay for them, would benefit indirectly if clearer substitution rules let cheaper interchangeable copies reach pharmacy shelves faster. Biosimilar manufacturers would also gain a clearer path to market.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to complete, within 12 months, a study of how the substitution of interchangeable biological products is affected by differences between the biologic interchangeability system and the generic drug therapeutic equivalence rating system.

Requires the FDA to report the study results to Congress and to update the Purple Book to harmonize how substitutability is communicated, with the stated goals of minimizing impediments to substitution while keeping the distinct approval pathways for biologics and drugs.
Interchangeable biologics can be substituted at the pharmacy without consulting the prescriber, like generic drugs, so clearer rules could put cheaper copies in patients' hands more often.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose prices are protected when cheaper interchangeable copies go unused, would bear the cost in the form of increased competition. Taxpayers fund the FDA study and report.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a study-and-update measure, not a mandate: even fully carried out, it would not directly lower any drug's price, and its main tool is revising how the Purple Book communicates information.
Substitution ultimately depends on state pharmacy laws and insurer formularies as well as federal listings, so harmonizing FDA communications may not change practice much on its own.

A good-faith objection is that biologics are complex products, and the distinct interchangeability standards exist partly for safety reasons; critics could argue against blurring the line with the simpler generic drug rating system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to patients is real but indirect and modest: the bill studies a barrier to substitution and tidies an FDA publication rather than mandating price relief or faster approvals. The cost is small (one federal study and report). An honest supporter would admit this is a first step, not a fix; an honest critic would note the narrow scope limited what it could achieve even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 24, 2023 by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks with a bipartisan group of cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and about a week later to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the legislative record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic makers are better off: nothing changed, so their exclusive control over pricing for widely prescribed biologics continues without the added substitution pressure this bill was designed to study. Patients continue to face the same barriers to cheaper interchangeable copies.

for.name: Reps. Barragán, Murphy, and Kuster
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a bipartisan, four-member cosponsor base (2 Democrats, 2 Republicans).

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; scheduled no hearing, no markup, and no vote on it, and it expired at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No opposition was ever recorded, and the small cosponsor group was evenly split between two Republicans and two Democrats, so the bill's fate reflects committee inaction rather than a party fight.

industries.note: These companies profit from biologics priced at hundreds or thousands of dollars per dose, and their revenue depends on cheaper interchangeable copies going unused. The bill targeted the communication barriers that slow substitution, so their interest in the bill ran against patients paying brand-name prices.

Clearer substitution rules and a harmonized Purple Book would make it easier for these firms' cheaper products to be dispensed in place of the originals. Their gain (more market access) lines up with patients' gain (lower prices).

industries.industry: Pharmacy chains and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Easier substitution can mean handling higher-value interchangeable products and more favorable reimbursement spreads, but also more complexity in managing which products are substitutable. The bill's study-first approach would not have changed their economics directly.
